text: The anaphoric demonstratives locate their referent not in space or time per se but rather in shared communicative context. In other words, they point back to a referent that has either been mentioned already in the same discourse or is already known by both speaker and hearer by some other means. Ik has a singular and a plural anaphoric demonstrative which are enclitics that have the same form in both non-final and final environments (i.e., their final vowels are not omitted). These invariant anaphoric demonstratives, translated into English as ‘that’ in the singular and ‘those’ in the plural, are presented in tab:dem:anaph : Ik anaphoric demonstratives also directly follow their referents, as in ex:dem:5 - ex:dem:6 :
summary: Anaphoric demonstratives refer to something in the shared communicative context rather than locating it in space or time; they point back to a referent already mentioned in discourse or otherwise known to both speaker and hearer. In Ik, there are singular and plural anaphoric demonstratives that are enclitic, invariant in both final and non-final environments, and directly follow their referents.

text: Besides the three types of nominal demonstratives described above, Ik also has a set of adverbial demonstratives that involve both locative and anaphoric locative reference. Unlike the nominal demonstratives, the adverbial demonstratives are technically nouns themselves in that they are marked for case and can take their own nominal demonstratives. Their function, however, is adverbial.
summary: Ik has a set of adverbial demonstratives in addition to the three nominal demonstrative types. These adverbial forms combine locative and anaphoric locative reference, are technically nouns because they can be case-marked and can take their own nominal demonstratives, but they function adverbially.

text: The first type of adverbial demonstrative, the locative adverbial demonstrative, locates the state or event expressed in a clause in physical space. Ik has three sets of such demonstratives. As shown in tab:dem:locadv , Sets 1 and 2 are built on degree of distance, while Set 3, in addition to degree of distance, is also split into singular and plural. These demonstratives are usually translated into English as ‘here’, ‘there’, and ‘over there’, depending on relative distance: Examples ex:dem:7 - ex:dem:8 illustrate the locative adverbial demonstratives:
summary: The passage describes the locative adverbial demonstrative, which places the state or event of a clause in physical space. Ik has three sets of these demonstratives: Sets 1 and 2 are organized by degree of distance, while Set 3 is additionally divided into singular and plural. They are typically translated as “here,” “there,” and “over there,” depending on relative distance.

text: The second type of Ik adverbial demonstrative are called the anaphoric locatives, which are nouns with a demonstrative function. Like the locative nominal demonstratives, these demonstratives point to a specific place – or metaphorically, a specific time – while also signifying anaphorically that that place or time is already known, either from earlier in the discourse or for some other reason. Ik has two such demonstratives with roughly the same meaning: tsʼ ' ɛ d ' ɛ - and tʉmɛd ' ɛ - , both of which are typically translated as ‘there’ or more rarely `then'. Because these words are technically nouns, tab:dem:locanaph presents them in a full case declension, while examples ex:dem:9 - ex:dem:10 illustrate them in sentences.
summary: Ik has two anaphoric locative demonstratives, tsʼɛdʼɛ- and tʉmɛdʼɛ-, which are nouns used with a demonstrative function. They point to a specific place or, metaphorically, a time, while also indicating that this referent is already known from the discourse or other context, and are typically translated as “there” or less often “then.”

text: Ik has a case system. This means that every noun has a special marking to show what role it has in the sentence. The language marks this role by means of a set of case suffixes (endings). Four of the cases are marked with suffixes consisting of a single vowel, while for three others, the suffix consists of /k/ plus a vowel. An eighth case, the oblique, is marked by the absence of any suffix. In the following examples, ex:case:1 - ex:case:8 , notice how the word ŋókí- ‘dog’ at the end of each sentence has a different ending depending on the case for which it is marked: Eight examples are given above because Ik has eight cases: nominative, accusative, dative , genitive, ablative, instrumental, copulative, and oblique. tab:case:suffixes presents the non-final and final forms of the suffixes that mark all eight of these cases. Keep in mind that the null symbol <Ø> signifies either 1) that the case suffix is inaudible or, for the oblique case , 2) that there is no case suffix: From tab:case:suffixes , there may appear to be significant ambiguity in the Ik case system. For instance, the non-final forms of the nominative and accusative suffixes, the dative and genitive suffixes, and the ablative, instrumental, and copulative suffixes all look the same, respectively. In most cases, the key to disambiguating the suffixes is called ‘subtractive’ morphology. Two of the Ik case suffixes (namely nominative and instrumental) are subtractive in that they subtract or delete the final vowel of the noun to which they attach. So, for example, while the non-final forms of the nominative and accusative are identical, their morphological behavior is not: the nominative -a subtracts the noun’s final vowel, as when ŋókí- ‘dog’ becomes ŋók-á ‘dog:nom’; by contrast, the accusative suffix is non-subtractive, as in ŋókí-à ‘dog:acc’. Other case ambiguities like genitive versus dative and ablative versus copulative, in their non-final forms, can be resolved in the context of the sentence. Different verbs require different cases. Since every Ik noun ends in a vowel, and since that vowel can be any of the nine (/i, ɨ, e, ɛ, a, ɔ, o, ʉ, u/), the collision of nouns and case suffixes gives rise to all kinds of vowel assimilation (see sec:2.4.4 ). The next two tables present declensions of two nouns illustrating vowel assimilation . tab:case:feti shows the noun fetí- ‘sun’ declined for all eight cases. In particular, notice how the vowel /o/ in the ablative and copulative suffixes partially assimilate the /i/ in fetí- to become /u/: While tab:case:feti shows partial vowel assimilation caused by case suffixation, tab:case:kija reveals an instance of total assimilation. In this table, the noun kíʝá- ‘land’ is declined for all eight cases. Note how the final /a/ of kíʝá- becomes totally assimilated by the non-final dative , genitive, ablative, and copulative suffixes.
summary:
Ik has eight cases—nominative, accusative, dative, genitive, ablative, instrumental, copulative, and oblique—marked by suffixes, with the oblique indicated by no suffix. Some case suffixes are ambiguous in form, but they can usually be distinguished by subtractive morphology, in which the nominative and instrumental delete the noun’s final vowel, and by the verbal or sentential context.  

Because Ik nouns end in vowels, attaching case suffixes often produces vowel assimilation; the passage illustrates both partial assimilation, as in *fetí-* ‘sun,’ and total assimilation, as in *kíʝá-* ‘land.’

text: The nominative case, marked by the suffix -a , is the ‘naming’ case, whose role is to: 1) mark the subject of main clauses, 2) mark the subject of sequential clauses (see sec:8.10.7 ), and 3) mark the direct object of clauses with 1 st and 2 nd person subjects (‘I’, ‘we’, ‘you’). Three examples ( ex:case:9 - ex:case:11 ) are provided below, each one illustrating one of the three grammatical roles of the nominative case . The third example contains seven sentences that show how Ik object marking is split: objects after 3-person subjects ((s)he/it, they) take the accusative case , while 1- or 2-person subjects (you, we) take objects in the nominative case : Subject of a main clause Subject of a sequential clause Object of a clause with a 1/2-person subject
summary: The nominative case, marked by the suffix **-a**, is used to mark subjects of main clauses and sequential clauses. It also marks direct objects when the subject is first or second person, while objects after third-person subjects take the accusative case.

text: The accusative case, marked by the suffix -ka , is also split with regard to its basic function. One of its basic functions, that for which it is named, is to mark the direct object of any clause with a 3-person subject ((s)he/it, they). Its other common function is to mark the subject and any object of several kinds of subordinate clauses (including relative and temporal clauses). Each of these functions is exemplified by one of the sentences in examples ex:case:12 - ex:case:15 . In the first example, a sentence with a 1-person subject is also given to show the contrast: Direct object of a clause with a 3-person subject Subject and object of a subordinate clause
summary: The accusative case, marked by the suffix **-ka**, has two main functions. It marks the direct object of clauses with a **third-person subject**, and it also marks the **subject and any object** in certain subordinate clauses, including relative and temporal clauses. The passage contrasts this use with a sentence containing a **first-person subject** to show the difference.

text: The dative case, marked by the suffix -ke , is the ‘to’ or ‘in’ case, whose role is to mark indirect objects (also called ‘extended’ or ‘secondary’ objects). These indirect objects may encode semantic notions like destination, location, recipient , experiencer, possession , and purpose. These are illustrated in examples ex:case:16 - ex:case:21 : Destination Location Recipient Experiencer Possession Purpose
summary: The dative case, marked by the suffix **-ke**, functions as the “to” or “in” case and is used to mark indirect objects, also called extended or secondary objects. These indirect objects can express several semantic roles, including destination, location, recipient, experiencer, possession, and purpose.

text: The genitive case, marked by the suffix -e , is the ‘of’ case, whose role is to encode a possessive or associative relationship a noun has with another noun (or, in rare cases, with a verb). Within the broad notions of possession and association are finer nuances such as: ownership, part-whole relationship, kinship, and attribution. These nuances are illustrated in examples ex:case:22 - ex:case:25 : Ownership Part-whole relationship Kinship Attribution The genitive case has two further roles. One is the nominalization of clauses, that is, the process by which a whole clause is changed into a noun phrase that can be used as a subject or object in another clause. For example, the clause Cɛɨƙɔta náa eakwa ídèmèk ᵃ ‘The man killed the snake’ can be compressed into the nominalized cɛ ' ɛ s ' ʉ ƙɔta eakwéé ídèmè ‘the killing of the man of the snake’ or ‘the man’s killing of the snake’. The other secondary role of the genitive has to do with verb ƙámón ‘to be like’. For unknown historical reasons, this particular verb requires genitive case marking on its complement , as in Ƙámá ròɓèè mùɲ ‘He’s like all people’, where ròɓè-è is analyzed as ‘people-gen’ or `of people'.
summary: The genitive case, marked by the suffix **-e**, mainly expresses possessive or associative relations between nouns, including ownership, part-whole relations, kinship, and attribution. It also has two additional uses: it can nominalize clauses so they function as noun phrases, and it marks the complement of the verb **ƙámón** “to be like,” which requires genitive case for historical reasons.

text: The ablative case, marked by the suffix -o , is the ‘from’ case (or in some situations `at' or `in'), whose function is to mark objects with the following semantic roles: origin/source, cause, stimulus, source of judgment, location of activity (versus static location, which is covered by the dative case). Each of these semantic roles of the ablative are illustrated among example sentences ex:case:26 - ex:case:30 : Origin/source Cause Stimulus Source of judgment Location of activity
summary: The ablative case, marked by the suffix **-o**, primarily expresses the “from” relation, though in some contexts it can mean “at” or “in.” It is used to mark nouns with roles such as **origin/source, cause, stimulus, source of judgment,** and **location of activity**, contrasting with the **dative case** for static location.

text: The instrumental case, marked by the suffix -o , is the ‘by’ or ‘with’ case. Unlike the ablative suffix -o , the instrumental suffix is subtractive, meaning that it first deletes the noun’s final vowel. The function of the instrumental case is to mark secondary objects with such semantic roles as instrument/means, pathway, accompaniment, manner, time, and occupation. Each of these nuances are illustrated by one sentence each in example sentences ex:case:31 - ex:case:36 : Instrument/means Pathway Accompaniment Manner Time Occupation
summary: The instrumental case, marked by the suffix **-o**, expresses the meanings of “by” or “with,” and unlike the ablative **-o** it is subtractive, first deleting the noun’s final vowel. It marks secondary objects with roles such as instrument or means, pathway, accompaniment, manner, time, and occupation.

text: The copulative case, marked by the suffix -ko , is the ‘is’ or ‘coupling’ case, whose function is to link one noun to another in a relationship of exact identity. In this function, the copulative marks three kinds of nouns: 1) a focused (fronted) noun, 2) the complement of a verbless copula (linking verb) clause, and 3) the complement of a negative copula of identity clause. These different uses of the copulative are illustrated in examples sentences ex:case:37 - ex:case:41 : Fronted subject Fronted object Fronted secondary object Verbless copula complement Negative copula complement
summary: The copulative case, marked by the suffix **-ko**, is used to link one noun to another in a relationship of exact identity. It marks three kinds of nouns: a focused or fronted noun, the complement of a verbless copula clause, and the complement of a negative copula of identity clause.

text: The oblique case, marked by the absence of any suffix, is the ‘leftover’ case. As such, it is employed to mark nouns in a variety of disparate grammatical roles and functions. Among these are the following: 1) The subject and/or object of an imperative clause, 2) the subject and/or object of an optative clause, 3) the object of a preposition , and 4) a vocative noun (used when calling someone). Each of these uses of the oblique case are demonstrated in examples ex:case:42 - ex:case:46 : Subject and/or object of an imperative clause Subject and/or object of an optative clause Object of a preposition Vocative
summary: The oblique case is the unmarked, “leftover” case with no suffix, and it is used for nouns in a range of different grammatical roles. These include the subject or object of imperative and optative clauses, the object of a preposition, and vocative nouns used in direct address.

text: Ik verbs consist of a verbal root (written in this book with a hyphen, as in wèt- ‘drink’) and at least one of a variety of available derivational and inflectional suffixes. The language has no prefixes except those borrowed centuries ago that no longer have any active function, for example the /a/ in áb ` ʉ b ` ʉ ƙ- ‘bubble’ or the /i/ in iɓóɓór- ‘hollow out’. Reduplicating a verb root, partially or totally, has long been a strategy for creating a sense of continuousness or repetitiveness, as when ɨtsán- ‘disturb’ becomes ɨtsan Í tsán- ‘torment relentlessly’. Ik employs a large number of suffixes to create longer verb stems. Among these are the infinitive and other deverbalizing suffixes that change a verb into a noun that can take case endings, demonstratives, relative clauses, etc. One very key verb-building strategy of Ik is the directional suffixes that signify the direction of the verb’s movement to or away from the speaker. These two directionals have also been extended metaphorically to express the beginning or completion of actions or processes. Another set of verbal suffixes deal with voice and valency, that is, the number of objects the verb requires. Among these are the passive, impersonal passive , middle, causative, and reciprocal. Once a verb is taken from the mental lexicon and used in speech, it often requires subject-agreement marking, which Ik accomplishes through pronominal suffixes. Ik also has a special verbal suffix, the dummy pronoun, that goes on the verb whenever a peripheral argument, like a place or time designation, has been moved to the front of the clause or removed entirely. The Ik verbal system has a variety of verbal paradigms based on mood and aspect. The basic distinction in mood is between realis and irrealis, or things that have happened and things that have not. Other modal distinctions include the optative, subjunctive, imperative, and negative. As for aspect , the specification of the internal structure of a verb – complete or incomplete – Ik has suffixes that mark present perfect, intentional -imperfective, pluractional, sequential, and simultaneous. Lastly, Ik exhibits a special set of adjectival suffixes to cover the language’s need to express adjectival concepts.
summary: Ik verbs are built from a verbal root plus one or more derivational and inflectional suffixes, since the language has no active prefixes and uses reduplication to mark continuous or repetitive action. The verbal system includes many suffixes for stem formation, direction, voice and valency, subject agreement, and mood/aspect distinctions such as realis/irrealis, optative, imperative, and several aspectual categories. Ik also has special suffixes for adjectival meanings and for marking displaced or omitted peripheral arguments.

text: intransitive verbs allow only a subject and possibly an indirect object – a direct object does not figure into their semantic schema. The Ik intransitive infinitive suffix is -ònì- . It converts an intransitive verb to a morphological noun that can be used as a noun in a noun phrase . The infinitive is the citation form of a verb, the form one cites in a dictionary or in isolation from other words. tab:verbs:intrans gives a few examples of intransitive infinitives from the lexicon: Because the infinitive is a noun morphologically, it can be fully declined for case as all nouns can. tab:verbs:intrans:case1 gives the case declension of the verb wàtònì- ‘to rain’, which shows some vowel assimilation effects on [+ ATR ] vowels, as when /io/ becomes /uo/ in the ablative and copulative cases. tab:verbs:intrans:case2 does the same for the [- ATR ] verb w ' ɛ d ` ɔ n Ì - ‘to detour’. Note /ɨɔ/ becoming /ʉɔ/ there as well:
summary: In Ik, intransitive verbs take only a subject and possibly an indirect object, with no direct object in their semantic structure. Their infinitive is formed with the suffix **-ònì-**, which turns the verb into a morphologically noun-like form used as the citation form and declined for case like other nouns. The passage also notes case declension examples showing vowel assimilation effects, including changes in [+ATR] and [-ATR] forms.

text: transitive verbs are those that admit a subject and a direct object into their schematic of an active event. The Ik transitive infinitive suffix is -ésí- . It converts a transitive verb to a morphological noun that can be used as a noun in a noun phrase . tab:verbs:trans1 presents a few examples of transitive infinitives: tab:verbs:trans2 gives the case declension of the deverbalized noun wetésí- ‘to drink’, which shows vowel assimilation effects on [+ ATR ] vowels. tab:verbs:trans3 does the same for the [- ATR ] verb for the [- ATR ] verb wɛtsʼ ' ɛ s Í - ‘to knap’.
summary: Transitive verbs are defined as those that take a subject and a direct object in an active-event schema, and in Ik the transitive infinitive suffix is **-ésí-**. This suffix turns a transitive verb into a morphological noun that can function as a noun phrase, and the examples show its case declension, including vowel assimilation with **[+ATR]** forms such as *wetésí-* ‘to drink’ and **[-ATR]** forms such as *wɛtsʼɛsÍ-* ‘to knap’.

text: semi-transitive verbs fall between transitive and intransitive in that they take an object, but the object is the reflexive pronoun as Í - ‘-self’, referring to the subject. This means that semi-transitive verbs are morphologically transitive but almost intransitive semantically. Another name for this is ‘middle’ (although see another Ik middle verb in sec:8.6.3 ). tab:verbs:semitrans provides a sample of semi-transitive verbs. No case declension is given for these because they decline the same way as the transitive infinitives shown in tab:verbs:trans2 and tab:verbs:trans3 :
summary: Semi-transitive verbs are described as intermediate between transitive and intransitive: they take an object, but that object is a reflexive pronoun meaning “-self” and referring back to the subject. Thus, they are morphologically transitive but semantically almost intransitive, and this type is also called “middle.” No separate case declension is given for them because they inflect like the transitive infinitives.

text: The abstractive suffix -ás Í - can be used to replace the intransitive suffix -ònì- for converting an intransitive verb to an abstract noun, for example, when hábòn ‘to be hot’ becomes hábàs ‘heat’. tab:verbs:abstr1 gives several examples of abstract nouns derived from intransitive verbs: Because verbs deverbalized by the abstractive suffix are morphological nouns, they are fully declined for case. tab:verbs:abstr2 gives one such case declension of the abstract noun kuɗás Í - ‘shortness’:
summary: The abstractive suffix **-ás Í-** can replace the intransitive suffix **-ònì-** to form abstract nouns from intransitive verbs, as in **hábòn** ‘to be hot’ becoming **hábàs** ‘heat’. These deverbalized forms are morphological nouns and therefore are fully declined for case, as shown by the declension of **kuɗás Í-** ‘shortness’.

text: The behaviorative suffix -nànèsì- is a complex suffix possibly consisting of the stative suffix -án- from sec:8.11.4 and the transitive suffix ( sec:8.2.2 ) or the abstractive suffix ( sec:8.3.1 ). Regardless of its composition, the suffix as a whole creates abstract concepts based on simple nouns, like ámánànès ‘personhood’ or ‘personality’ from ámá- ‘person’. tab:verbs:behave1 provides a few more examples: Because behavioratives are nouns morphologically, they are declined for case. tab:verbs:behave2 gives the case declension for the word eakwánánèsì - ‘manhood’:
summary: The behaviorative suffix -nànèsì- is a complex suffix, possibly made up of the stative suffix -án- plus either the transitive or abstractive suffix, though its exact composition is uncertain. It forms abstract nouns from simple nouns, such as ámánànès ‘personhood/personality’ from ámá- ‘person’, and these behaviorative nouns are inflected for case, as shown by the declension of eakwánánèsì ‘manhood’.

text: The patientive suffix -amá- converts a verb to a noun that is characterized by the meaning of the verb. It is called ‘patientive’ because the derived noun usually has the meaning of ‘ patient ’ or object of the original verb, as when meetés ‘to give’ produces meetam ‘gift’. tab:verbs:pat1 gives some examples of patientive nouns: Because patientives are nouns morphologically, they are fully declined for case. tab:verbs:pat2 gives the full declension of the noun wetamá- ‘drink(able)’:
summary: The patientive suffix **-amá-** turns a verb into a noun whose meaning is based on the verb, usually referring to the patient or object of the action, as in **meetés** ‘to give’ becoming **meetam** ‘gift’. Since patientives are morphologically nouns, they are fully declined for case.

text: The venitive suffix -ét- denotes a direction toward a deictic center, usually (but not always) the speaker. It can be translated variously as ‘here’, ‘this way’, ‘out’, or ‘up’, but it is the Middle English word ‘hither’ that captures its essence nicely. The venitive suffix comes between the verb root and the infinitive suffix, whether intransitive or transitive. It can be used to augment any verb whose meaning includes motion or movement of any kind. tab:verbs:ven gives a few examples: Venitive infinitives are morphological nouns and thus are declined for case. See sec:8.2.1 and sec:8.2.2 for case declensions that show the relevant endings.
summary: The venitive suffix **-ét-** marks movement toward a deictic center, usually the speaker, and is roughly comparable to English **“hither,”** with meanings such as “here,” “this way,” “out,” or “up.” It appears between the verb root and the infinitive suffix, can be added to verbs involving motion or movement, and venitive infinitives are morphological nouns that decline for case.

text: The andative suffix -uƙot(í)- denotes direction away from a deictic center, usually the speaker (but not always). It can be translated variously as ‘away’, ‘off’, ‘out’, ‘that way’, or ‘there’, but it is the Middle English word ‘thither’ that captures its essence nicely. Unlike the venitive suffix, the andative comes after both the verbal root and the infinitive suffix (in an infinitival construction). It can be used to augment any verb whose meaning includes motion or movement of any kind. tab:verbs:and1 provides a few examples of andative verbs. Because the andative suffix comes after infinitive suffixes, whenever an andative infinitive is declined for case, it is the andative suffix that takes case endings. tab:verbs:and2 gives a declension of the [+ ATR ] andative verb séɓésuƙotí- ‘to sweep off’, while tab:verbs:and3 does the same for the [- ATR ] verb sɛk ' ɛ s ' ʉ ƙɔt Í - ‘to scrub off’:
summary: The andative suffix **-uƙot(í)-** marks motion away from a deictic center, usually the speaker, with meanings such as ‘away,’ ‘off,’ ‘out,’ ‘that way,’ or ‘there.’ It follows both the verbal root and, in infinitival constructions, the infinitive suffix, and it can be added to verbs involving motion; when an andative infinitive is declined for case, the case endings attach to the andative suffix itself.

text: The inchoative suffix -ét- is identical to the venitive suffix described in sec:8.4.1 , and this is because its meaning is a metaphorical extension of the meaning of the venitive. That is, the venitive meaning of ‘hither’ was extended to mean the beginning of a state or activity (for intransitives) or the starting up of some action or process (for transitives). The inchoative behaves morphologically (including case declensions) exactly the same as the venitive. tab:verbs:inch gives a few examples of intransitive and transitive verbs in the inchoative aspect :
summary: The inchoative suffix -ét- is identical in form to the venitive suffix because its meaning developed as a metaphorical extension of the venitive sense of ‘hither.’ This extension came to mark the beginning of a state or activity in intransitive verbs and the starting of an action or process in transitive verbs. Morphologically, including in its case declensions, the inchoative behaves exactly like the venitive.

text: The completive suffix -uƙot(í)- is identical to the andative suffix described in sec:8.4.2 , and this is because its meaning is a metaphorical extension of the meaning of the andative . That is, the andative meaning of ‘thither’ was extended to mean the completion of a change of state or activity (for intransitives) or the fulfillment of some action or process (for transitives). The completive behaves morphologically (including case declensions) exactly the same as the andative . tab:verbs:comp gives a few examples of lexical verbs in the completive aspect :
summary: The completive suffix **-uƙot(í)-** is formally identical to the andative suffix because its meaning developed as a metaphorical extension of the andative ‘thither.’ This extension came to express completion of a change of state or activity with intransitives, and the fulfillment of an action or process with transitives. Morphologically, including case declensions, the completive behaves exactly like the andative.

text: The pluractional suffix -í- denotes an action or state that is construed as inherently plural in its realization. This notion of plurality can mean any of the following: 1) an intransitive action done more than once or done by more than one subject, 2) a state attributed more than once or of more than one subject, 3) a transitive action done more than once, done by more than one subject, or done to more than one object. In short, the pluractional suffix conveys the idea that the application of the verb is multiple. The pluractional suffix comes just before the infinitive suffix and is a dominant [+ ATR ] suffix that harmonizes [- ATR ] vowels. tab:verbs:pluract gives a few examples of intransitive and transitive pluractional verbs:
summary: The pluractional suffix **-í-** marks an action or state as inherently plural in its realization, meaning it can indicate repetition, multiple subjects, or multiple objects depending on the verb type. It generally conveys that the verb applies multiple times or in multiple instances. The suffix occurs just before the infinitive suffix and is a dominant **[+ATR]** suffix that harmonizes **[-ATR]** vowels.

text: The Ik passive suffix -ósí- has the unusual distinction of being able to modify both intransitive and transitive verbs. With intransitive verbs, it adds the nuance of characteristicness to the meaning of the verb, often with the help of root reduplication . With transitive verbs, it has the usual function of a passive , which is to convert the object of a transitive verb into the subject of an intransitive verb. tab:verbs:pass gives examples of both intransitive and transitive passives: Another quirky feature of the Ik passive -ósí- is that it can function both as a passive infinitive suffix (taking case) and as a regular inflectional suffix followed by subject-agreement pronouns. When it is declined for case, it declines just like the transitive suffix -ésí- in sec:8.2.2 . Example ex:verbs:1 below illustrates this in a sentence where the passive infinitive búdòsì- ‘to be hidden’ gets the accusative case . Then, example ex:verbs:2 shows the same passive acting as a verb proper, taking the 3pl subject-agreement pronominal suffix -át- :
summary: The Ik passive suffix **-ósí-** is unusual because it can attach to both intransitive and transitive verbs: with intransitives it adds a sense of characteristicness, often with root reduplication, and with transitives it has the normal passive function of promoting the object to subject. It is also distinctive in that it can behave either as a **passive infinitive suffix** that takes case or as a regular inflectional suffix followed by subject-agreement pronouns.

text: The impersonal passive suffix -àn- behaves like a typical passive in that it eliminates the agent of a transitive verb and promotes the object to subject. However, unlike the passive -ósí- described above, the impersonal passive cannot be specified for the person or number of its subject. Instead, it remains marked for 3sg regardless of who or what the subject may be. Another strange property of - ` a n- is that it can be used with intransitive verbs as well (just like the passive ). When used with intransitive verbs, it has the function of downplaying the identity of the subject. For this reason, it can often be translated as ‘People ’ or ‘One ’, as in Tódian ‘People say (it)’. The impersonal passive is a grammatical morpheme not listed in the lexicon, and so it must be illustrated in examples like ex:verbs:3 - ex:verbs:4 :
summary: The impersonal passive suffix **-àn-** functions like a typical passive by removing the agent of a transitive verb and promoting the object to subject. Unlike the passive **-ósí-**, however, it is always marked **3sg** and cannot be specified for the person or number of its subject. It can also occur with intransitive verbs, where it downplays the identity of the subject and may be translated as **“people”** or **“one.”**

text: Ik has two middle suffixes: -m- and -ím- . Like the semi-transitive construction discussed in sec:8.2.3 , the middle suffixes convert simple transitive verbs into something in the ‘middle’ of transitive and intransitive . That is, the Ik middle verbs convey that idea that if an action is done to an entity, it is the entity itself – if anything – doing it to itself alone, apart from any other explicit agent. The middles eliminate the agent and promote the patient to subject. The middle suffix -m- always has a vowel between it and the preceding verb root. This vowel is usually a copy of the root vowel, as when ɗusés ‘cut’ becomes ɗusúmón ‘to cut (alone/on its own)’, but it can also have a non-copy vowel as in bokímón ‘to get caught’. For its part, the middle suffix -ím- – a dominant [+ ATR ] suffix – is always paired with the inchoative suffix -ét- , thereby forming the complex morpheme -ímét- . tab:verbs:middle below gives some examples of these two suffixes converting transitive verbs to middle verbs.
summary: Ik has two middle suffixes, -m- and -ím-, which turn simple transitive verbs into middle verbs, eliminating the agent and promoting the patient to subject. The -m- suffix always takes an intervening vowel, usually copied from the root vowel but sometimes not, while -ím- always occurs together with the inchoative suffix -ét-, forming the complex morpheme -ímét-.

text: The reciprocal suffix -ínósí- denotes a reciprocal relationship that a verb’s subject has with itself. That is, the reciprocal collapses the subject and direct object of a transitive verb, or the subject and a secondary object of an intransitive verb, into just the subject of a reciprocal verb. In this regard, it is similar to the semi-transitive verbs from sec:8.2.3 that use the reflexive pronoun as Í - ‘-self’. tab:verbs:recip1 provides a few examples of reciprocals derived from other verbs: Like the passive -ósí- discussed in sec:8.6.1 , the reciprocal suffix can take either case endings (as a morphological noun) or subject-agreement endings (as a morphological verb). A case declension of ínínósí- ‘to cohabitate’ is shown in tab:verbs:recip2 , and in example ex:verbs:5 below, the reciprocal verb ɨɓák Í n ' ɔ s Í - ‘to be next to each other’ gets the accusative case . Then, example ex:verbs:6 shows the same verb acting as a verb proper, with the 3pl subject-agreement marker -át- :
summary:
The reciprocal suffix **-ínósí-** marks a situation in which the subject acts in a reciprocal relation with itself, collapsing the subject and object roles of a transitive verb, or the subject and secondary object of an intransitive verb, into a single subject. It is similar to semi-transitive verbs using the reflexive pronoun **Í-** ‘-self’.  

Like the passive suffix **-ósí-**, the reciprocal can function either as a morphological noun with case endings or as a morphological verb with subject-agreement endings, as shown by examples such as **ínínósí-** ‘to cohabitate’ and **ɨɓákínósí-** ‘to be next to each other.’

text: Ik expresses causativity with a morphological causative , the causative suffix -ìt- . When this suffix is added to a verb with meaning X, it changes the meaning of the verb to ‘cause/make (to) X’. This suffix can be used to causativize intransitive and transitive verbs and comes right after the verb root, before the infinitive marker (if present) and any other suffixes like an inchoative or pluractional. If the last vowel of the verb root is /u/, the causative may be assimilated to the form -ùt- . tab:verbs:caus gives several examples of causativized verbs.
summary: Ik forms causatives with the suffix **-ìt-**, which changes a verb meaning X into one meaning ‘cause/make (to) X’. This suffix can attach to both intransitive and transitive verbs, appearing immediately after the verb root and before the infinitive marker or other suffixes. If the final vowel of the root is **/u/**, the causative may surface as **-ùt-**.

text: Whenever Ik grammar requires verbs to agree with their subjects, one of the seven pronominal suffixes in tab:verbs:subj are used. Note that if the verb contains [- ATR ] vowels, these suffixes will also be harmonized to [- ATR ]. Just like the free pronouns described back in sec:5.2 , these bound pronominal suffixes are organized along three axes: 1) person (1/2/3), 2) number (singular/plural), and 3) clusivity (exclusive/inclusive). The form these pronominals ultimately take depends on the grammatical mood of the verb to which they attach. If the verb is in the irrealis mood (see sec:8.9.1 ), the suffixes appear with their underlying forms. Whereas if they are in the realis mood (see sec:8.9.2 ), the realis suffix -a first subtracts or deletes their final vowel. The difference in the two mood-based paradigms is depicted in tab:verbs:subj . To see instances of the Ik subject-agreement suffixes in actual language use, you may refer back to example ex:case:11 in sec:7.2 .
summary: Ik verbs that agree with their subjects use one of seven pronominal suffixes, which are organized by person, number, and clusivity. These suffixes harmonize to [-ATR] when attached to verbs with [-ATR] vowels, and their final shape depends on mood: in the irrealis they appear in their underlying forms, while in the realis mood the suffix -a deletes their final vowel.

text: Ik has a special verbal affix called the dummy pronoun because it represents a secondary (indirect) object that has been (re)moved. That is, the dummy pronoun is a form of object-marking on the verb, but not of direct object marking. For example, if an indirect object expressing location or time or means is moved to the front of a clause for emphasis, it leaves a trace on the verb in the form of the dummy pronoun . Seen from another perspective, the dummy pronoun is always a clue that there is a missing syntactic constituent in the clause. The dummy pronoun has the form - ' dè and is very volatile in terms of allomorphy , dramatically changing its form in different morpho-phonological environments. Once the /d/ is lost in non-final forms, vowel assimilation and vowel harmony so distort the dummy pronoun as to make it almost unrecognizable at times. tab:verbs:dummy below is given to illustrate its diverse allomorphy : Examples ex:verbs:7 - ex:verbs:8 illustrate the dummy pronoun in two different morphological forms: final and non-final. Note that the tones associated with the pronoun in these examples do not match what is shown in tab:verbs:dummy ; this is because of local tonal interference. In terms of function, the dummy pronoun in ex:verbs:7 indicates that an indirect object – the destination of the verb ƙáátà ‘they go (went)’ – has been displaced from its usual spot after the verb to a place of focus at the beginning of the sentence (Ntsúó). Then in ex:verbs:8 , the dummy pronoun marks an indirect object – the location of staying – that is missing from the clause entirely. Since this sentence was taken out of context from a story, most likely the missing object had been already mentioned earlier in the discourse:
summary: Ik has a special verbal affix called the dummy pronoun, which marks a displaced or missing indirect object rather than a direct object. It appears when an indirect object such as a location, time, or means is moved to sentence-initial focus or is omitted entirely, and it has several highly variable allomorphs shaped by morphophonological processes.

text: A basic distinction in grammatical mood cleaves Ik verbal aspects and modalities right down the center, and this distinction is between irrealis and realis. As it applies specifically to Ik, the irrealis mood includes states and events whose actuality or reality are not expressly encoded in the grammar. Another way of saying this is that irrealis verbs in Ik can convey anything but whether a state or event has happened, is happening, or will happen. The morphological manifestation of the irrealis is that the final suffix of an irrealis verb – a subject-agreement pronoun – surfaces with its underlying form (see tab:verbs:subj ). The verbal aspects and modalities that fall under the irrealis mood include the optative, subjunctive, imperative, negative, sequential, and simultaneous.
summary: Ik grammar distinguishes sharply between irrealis and realis mood. In Ik, irrealis marks states or events whose actuality is not explicitly encoded, so irrealis verbs do not specify whether something has happened, is happening, or will happen; morphologically, the final subject-agreement suffix appears in its underlying form. The irrealis mood includes the optative, subjunctive, imperative, negative, sequential, and simultaneous aspects/modalities.

text: In contrast to irrealis, the realis mood includes states and events whose actuality or reality are encoded in the grammar. That is to say, realis verbs in Ik include in their meaning the fact that something has taken place, is taking place, or will take place in the real world. The morphological manifestation of the realis mood is seen in the realis suffix -a that subtracts or deletes the final vowel of the subject-agreement suffix to which it attaches (again, see tab:verbs:subj ). In terms of verb types, the realis mood includes declarative statements in the past or non-past, questions about the past or non-past, and, rather paradoxically, negative imperatives (which one might expect to fall under irrealis).
summary: The realis mood in Ik marks states and events as actual in the grammar, meaning that something has taken place, is taking place, or will take place in the real world. It is expressed by the suffix **-a**, which removes the final vowel of the subject-agreement suffix it attaches to. Realis forms include declarative and interrogative clauses in both past and non-past, as well as negative imperatives.

text: The intentional-imperfective aspect suffix -és- has two functions, hence its hyphenated title. One is to denote either an intention on the part of animate subjects or an imminence on the part of inanimate subjects. It is in this role that it finds use as the usual translation for the English future tense . It is also the answer to the question, “How do you express future tense in Ik?” A second function is to denote grammatical imperfectivity: a sense that a state or event is ongoing or incomplete. The two concepts collapse into one when intention/imminence is viewed as the incomplete coming-to-be of a future state or event. And even though intention or imperfectivity may seem to fall under an irrealis mood, -és- can actually be used with verbs in either the realis or irrealis mood. In tab:verbs:int , -és- is illustrated with the verb àts- ‘come’ in its imperfective sense with a recent past tense marker (nák ᵃ) and then in its intentional (English `future') sense:
summary: The suffix **-és-** has two functions: it can express **intention** in animate subjects or **imminence** in inanimate subjects, and it can also mark **grammatical imperfectivity**, meaning an ongoing or incomplete state or event. These meanings are related because intention or imminence can be understood as the incomplete coming-to-be of a future event, and the suffix can occur with verbs in either the **realis** or **irrealis** mood.

text: The Ik present perfect suffix - ' ka denotes a state or event recently completed (‘perfected’) but still relevant in the present. The suffix has a ‘floating’ high tone that shows up on the preceding syllable of 3sg verbs, for example in Nabʉƙɔták ᵃ ‘It is finished’. The /k/ in - ' ka disappears in non-final environments, making - ' a an allomorph. tab:verbs:perf presents the paradigm of the present perfect with the verb àts- ‘come’ in both non-final and final environments:
summary: In Ik, the present perfect suffix **-'ka** marks a state or event that has been recently completed and is still relevant to the present. It carries a floating high tone that appears on the preceding syllable in 3sg verbs, and its /k/ is lost in non-final environments, yielding the allomorph **-'a**.

text: The Ik optative mood is used to express wishes, even ironic ones like ‘Let the enemies comeǃ’. Optative verbs are often introduced with imperative verbs like ' O goe or Taláké, both of which mean ‘Let ’. And all Ik optative verbs are translated into English with a sentence beginning with ‘Let ’ or ‘May ’. Morphologically, the optative is marked by a combination of tone and special irregular suffixes. All optative verbs except 3pl show a kind of high-tone ‘leveling’ in the subject-agreement suffixes. The leveled high tone is pushed out to the end, creating a floating high tone. This high tone is not seen except in the fact that the last syllable of the subject-agreement suffixes remains at mid-tone level. Besides tone, special irregular suffixes mark the optative in 1sg, 1pl.exc, and 1pl.inc verbs, while standard irrealis suffixes are used for the other paradigm members. Note that the 1pl.inc may also be called the ‘hortative’. Another peculiarity of the Ik optative is that there is no difference between its non-final and final forms. tab:verbs:opt presents the optative on the verb àts- ‘come’:
summary: The Ik optative mood expresses wishes, including ironic ones, and is typically translated with English sentences beginning “Let” or “May.” It is marked by a combination of tone and irregular suffixes: most optative forms show high-tone leveling in the subject-agreement suffixes, with special suffixes in 1sg, 1pl.exc, and 1pl.inc, while other forms use standard irrealis suffixes. Unlike other forms, the optative does not distinguish between non-final and final forms.

text: The Ik subjunctive mood is used to encode statements that are somehow contingent or temporally unrealized. In that regard, it is an essentially irrealis verb form because it captures states or events that have not yet happened. It is also essentially irrealis in that it is marked simply by the absence of any marking. In other words, the subject-agreement suffixes surface with their underlying forms in the subjunctive mood , just as they appear in tab:verbs:subj . The subjunctive is usually introduced either by ɗɛmʉsʉ ‘unless, until’ or damu (kóʝa) ‘may’. tab:verbs:subjct gives the full subjunctive paradigm with the verb àts- ‘come’:
summary: The Ik subjunctive mood expresses contingent or temporally unrealized situations, so it functions as an irrealis form for events or states that have not yet happened. It is marked only by the absence of special overt marking, with subject-agreement suffixes appearing in their underlying forms. The subjunctive is usually introduced by ɗɛmʉsʉ ‘unless, until’ or damu (kóʝa) ‘may’.

text: The imperative mood is used to issue commands or instructions. If the recipient of the command is singular, then the suffix used is -e ' , and if the recipient is plural, the suffix is -úó . The singular -e ' has a floating high tone that raises any preceding low tones to mid. Both imperative suffixes are appended to the end of the verb stem, and no subject-agreement markers are needed. Both imperative suffixes are subject to vowel devoicing before a pause, as shown in tab:verbs:imp :
summary: The imperative mood is used for commands or instructions, with the singular marked by the suffix **-e'** and the plural by **-úó**. The singular suffix has a floating high tone that raises any preceding low tones to mid, and both imperative suffixes attach to the end of the verb stem without any subject-agreement markers. Both suffixes also undergo vowel devoicing before a pause.

text: Ik negates clauses by means of verblike particles that come first in the negative clause. If the negated clause has a realis verb, then the negator particle used is ńtá ‘not’. If the negated clause has an irrealis verb, then the negator particle is mòò or nòò. Lastly, if the negated clause is past tense realis or present perfect realis, then the negator particle used is máà or náà. In the negated clause, the negator particle comes first, followed by the subject, and then the verb. Any negated verb takes the irrealis mood with the appropriate form of subject-agreement suffixes (see tab:verbs:subj ). To make all this more concrete, tab:verbs:neg gives example of the different negator particles used with different types of clauses.
summary: Ik negation is expressed with clause-initial verblike particles: ńtá for realis clauses, mòò or nòò for irrealis clauses, and máà or náà for past tense realis or present perfect realis clauses. In negative clauses, the order is negator plus subject plus verb, and the negated verb appears in the irrealis mood with the appropriate subject-agreement suffixes.

text: The Ik sequential aspect expresses states or events that happen in sequence. Usually a sequence of verbs starts with an anchoring non-sequential verb and/or time expression , and then a clause chain begins in the sequential aspect . For example, when someone tells a story, they may start with one or two past tense realis verbs to set the stage and then continue the narrative with sequential verbs. Or if someone is giving a set of instructions, they may start with one or two imperative verbs followed by a chain of sequential verbs. Because of its versatility, the Ik sequential aspect is the language’s most frequently used verb form. Morphologically, Ik sequential verbs are recognized by a combination of tone, irregular subject-agreement suffixes, and the sequential aspect suffix -ko . Specifically, all 1 and 2-person sequential verbs exhibit high-tone leveling in their subject-agreement suffixes, which pushes a high tone out to the right of the verb. This floating high raises the preceding low tones to mid. These tone effects, plus the irregular suffixes, and the sequential marker -ko are shown in tab:verbs:seq . Note that the sequential paradigm also has an impersonal passive marked with the suffix -ese . Its function is identical to that of the impersonal passive described back in sec:8.6.2 . For more on how the sequential aspect works in actual language contexts, skip ahead to the discussion of clause-chaining in sec:10.8.2 .
summary: The Ik sequential aspect is used to express events or states in sequence, typically following an initial anchoring verb or time expression and then continuing a narrative or set of instructions in a clause chain. It is the language’s most frequently used verb form, and sequential verbs are identified by tone patterns, irregular subject-agreement suffixes, and the suffix **-ko**; the paradigm also includes an impersonal passive in **-ese**.

text: The Ik simultaneous aspect is used to express states or events that are happening simultaneously to another state or event. In contrast to the sequential, the simultaneous aspect can only be used in subordinate clauses. That is to say, simultaneous clauses usually cannot stand alone without a main clause (with some exceptions). Because of its role of supporting sequential clauses, the simultaneous aspect is also commonly found in narratives and other longer discourses. It can be given a perfective interpretation as in ‘when I came’ or an imperfective one as in ‘while I was coming’. Morphologically, the simultaneous aspect is marked by the suffix -ke , which is affixed to the subject-agreement suffixes in their irrealis forms. tab:verbs:sim presents the simultaneous paradigm of àts- ‘come’:
summary: The Ik simultaneous aspect expresses a state or event occurring at the same time as another, and it is used only in subordinate clauses rather than as a standalone clause, with a few exceptions. It is common in narratives and other extended discourse because it supports sequential clauses, and it can be interpreted either perfectively (“when I came”) or imperfectively (“while I was coming”). Morphologically, it is marked by the suffix **-ke**, attached to subject-agreement suffixes in their irrealis forms.

text: Since Ik does not have a separate word class of adjectives, it conveys adjectival concepts with adjectival verbs . These verbs have adjectival meanings but otherwise mostly behave like intransitive verbs. One way they do differ from normal intransitive verbs, though, is in the specific adjectival suffixes they can take. The next four subsections briefly describe these special adjectival suffixes.
summary: Ik lacks a separate class of adjectives, so adjectival meanings are expressed through adjectival verbs. These verbs generally behave like intransitive verbs, but they differ in the special adjectival suffixes they can take, which are described in the following subsections.

text: The physical property i adjectival suffix - ' d- is found on adjectival verbs that express physical properties like appearance, size, shape, consistency, texture, and other tangible attributes. As a result, physical property I verbs are some of the language’s most colorful adjectivals. Physical property I verbs all contain two syllables with LH tone pattern, and in the infinitive , they take the intransitive suffix -ònì- . tab:verbs:phys1 gives a sample of these colorful descriptive terms:
summary: The adjectival suffix **-’d-** appears on verbs describing physical properties such as appearance, size, shape, consistency, texture, and other tangible qualities, making these among the language’s most vivid adjectival forms. These **physical property I** verbs are all **disyllabic with an LH tone pattern**, and in the infinitive they take the **intransitive suffix -ònì-**.

text: The physical property ii adjectival suffix -m- is found in adjectival verbs that also express physical properties like appearance, color, consistency, posture, shape, and texture. It can also express less tangible attributes like strength, weakness, quality, or personality traits. Physical property II verbs usually contain two syllables with a LH tone pattern or three syllables with a LHH tone pattern (without the infinitive suffix), and in the infinitive , they take the intransitive suffix -ònì . tab:verbs:phys2 gives a sample of these descriptive adjectival verbs in two groupings.
summary: The adjectival suffix **-m-** occurs in verbs expressing physical properties such as appearance, color, consistency, posture, shape, and texture, and it can also extend to less concrete qualities like strength, weakness, quality, and personality traits. These Physical Property II verbs typically have either two syllables with an **LH** tone pattern or three syllables with an **LHH** pattern, and in the infinitive they take the intransitive suffix **-ònì**.

text: The stative adjectival suffix -án- forms adjectival verbs that express an ongoing state characterized by the meaning of a noun or a transitive verb. Because -án- contains the vowel /a/, it prevents vowel harmony from spreading between the verbal root and any suffixes that follow the stative suffix (for example, infinitive or subject-agreement suffixes). tab:verbs:stat1 and tab:verbs:stat2 present a few examples of stative adjectival verbs derived from nouns and verbs, respectively:
summary: The stative adjectival suffix **-án-** creates adjectival verbs expressing an ongoing state based on the meaning of a noun or a transitive verb. Because it contains the vowel **/a/**, it blocks vowel harmony from spreading between the verbal root and any following suffixes, such as infinitive or subject-agreement markers.

text: Ik has two distributive adjectival suffixes: -aák- and -ìk- . These suffixes have the function of distributing the meaning of an adjectival verb to more than one subject. The suffix -aák- can be used with all kinds of adjectival verbs, including the physical property and stative varieties, while the suffix -ìk- has been found only with the two verbs of size, kwáts- ‘small’ and zè- ‘large’. Moreover, it commonly occurs together with -aák- , as in kwátsíkaakón ‘to be small (of many)’ and zeikaakón ‘to be large (of many)’. tab:verbs:distr gives a sampling of adjectival verbs with the distributive suffix:
summary: Ik has two distributive adjectival suffixes, **-aák-** and **-ìk-**, which spread the meaning of an adjectival verb across more than one subject. The suffix **-aák-** occurs with all kinds of adjectival verbs, including physical property and stative verbs, whereas **-ìk-** is attested only with the size verbs **kwáts-** ‘small’ and **zè-** ‘large’. In addition, **-ìk-** commonly appears together with **-aák-**, as in forms meaning ‘to be small (of many)’ and ‘to be large (of many)’.

text: The word class called adverbs is a catch-all category that includes words and clitics of various sorts that say something descriptive about a whole clause, for example, ‘how’ or ‘when’ it takes place, or how the speaker feels about the certainty or contingency of the clause. Accordingly, Ik adverbs can be divide up into manner adverbs, temporal adverbs, and epistemic adverbs. The following subsections take up each of these adverbial categories in a brief discussion.
summary: Adverbs are described as a broad catch-all word class including words and clitics that provide descriptive information about an entire clause, such as how or when an event occurs, or the speaker’s assessment of its certainty or contingency. In Ik, adverbs are divided into three types: manner, temporal, and epistemic adverbs. The passage says that the following sections will briefly discuss each of these categories.

text: manner adverbs modify whole clauses by commenting on, for example, the manner in which a state comes across or in which an action is done. Manner adverbs usually come near or at the end of the clause they modify, as shown in example sentences ex:adv:1 - ex:adv:2 below. tab:adv:manner presents a sampling of these adverbs:
summary: Manner adverbs modify whole clauses by describing the manner in which a state appears or an action is carried out. They usually occur near or at the end of the clause they modify, and the passage notes that a table provides examples of such adverbs.

text: The Ik temporal adverbs situate their clause somewhere in the course of time. Ik has sets of temporal adverbs that deal with past tense , past perfect tense , and non-past (including future) tense . The past and past perfect tense adverbs are enclitics that come directly after the verb they modify. The future tense adverbs are free adverbs that come near the end or at the end of the clause.
summary: Ik temporal adverbs place the clause at a point in time, and the language has separate sets for past, past perfect, and non-past (including future) reference. The past and past perfect adverbs are enclitics attached directly after the verb, while future tense adverbs are free forms that appear near the end or at the end of the clause.

text: Ik divides past tense into four time periods and marks them with adverbial enclitics. They are: 1) recent past that covers the current day and is marked with =nákà, 2) removed past that covers yesterday (or any last or ‘yester-’ time period like 'yesterday' or 'yesteryear') and is marked with =bàtsè, 3) remote past that covers a few days or weeks before yesterday and is marked with =nótsò, and finally, 4) remotest past that covers everything before the remote past and is marked with =nòkò. Each of these tense enclitics comes directly after ther verb and has a non-final and final form. tab:adv:past illustrates the Ik tense markers in all their forms, and examples ex:adv:3 - ex:adv:4 illustrate their typical post-verbal position in a sentence:
summary: Ik divides past tense into four time periods, each marked by a post-verbal adverbial enclitic: recent past (=nákà) for the current day, removed past (=bàtsè) for yesterday or similar “yester-” periods, remote past (=nótsò) for a few days or weeks before yesterday, and remotest past (=nòkò) for everything earlier. Each enclitic has both a non-final and a final form, and it appears directly after the verb.

text: The past tense can be combined with a perfect aspect to yield the past perfect tense . Unlike the simple past tense adverbs, Ik past perfect tense adverbs operate along only three periods of time: recent (earlier today), removed (yester-), and remote (before yester-). tab:adv:prf presents the Ik past perfect tense adverbs, and example sentences ex:adv:5 - ex:adv:6 illustrate their use in natural contexts:
summary: The past tense can combine with perfect aspect to form the past perfect tense. In Ik, past perfect tense adverbs are organized into three time periods only: recent (earlier today), removed (yesterday), and remote (before yesterday).

text: Ik divides the non-past tense into three rather vaguely defined time periods suggested by three adverbs. They are: 1) the distended present that includes just before and just after the present and is expressed by the adverb tsʼ ` ɔ ` ɔ , 2) the removed future that includes the next future time period (next hour, next day, next year) and is expressed by the adverb táá, and 3) the remote future expressed by the adverb fàrà (occasionally fàrò). tab:adv:npst arranges these adverbs in a paradigm, while ex:adv:7 - ex:adv:8 below illustrates them in natural sentences:
summary: Ik divides the non-past tense into three vaguely defined temporal periods, each associated with a specific adverb: the distended present, expressed by tsʼ ɔ ɔ, the removed future, expressed by táá, and the remote future, expressed by fàrà (occasionally fàrò). The passage says that these adverbs are arranged in a paradigm and illustrated in natural sentences.

text: The Ik epistemic adverbs express how the speaker feels or thinks about the certainty or contingency of the clause. Accordingly, this set of adverbs can be divided into the categories of inferential, confirmational, and conditional-hypothetical. All of the epistemic adverbs are enclitics that follow the verb in normal main clauses, but some of them can also be moved in front of the verb.
summary: Ik epistemic adverbs indicate the speaker’s assessment of a clause’s certainty or contingency and are divided into inferential, confirmational, and conditional-hypothetical types. They are enclitics that normally follow the verb in main clauses, though some can also be placed before the verb.

text: Ik can communicate a degree of un certainty about a situation by means of a set of inferential tense-based adverbs. This sense of making a tentative inference based on an observation can be translated into English with such turns of phrase as ‘Apparently ’, ‘Maybe ’, ‘It seems that ’, ‘must have’, etc. Two of these inferential particles consist of the proclitic ná plus a past- tense particle , while the third combines ná with the adverb tsamʉ. tab:adv:inf presents the three inferential adverbial particles in their final and non-final forms. Note that compared to the past- tense markers above in tab:adv:past , the inferential time-scale is moved up one notch more recent. Examples ex:adv:9 - ex:adv:10 show the Ik inferential adverbs in context. Note that they can be placed before or after the main verb.
summary: Ik uses a set of inferential, tense-based adverbs to express tentative conclusions or uncertainty based on observation, roughly comparable to English forms like “apparently,” “maybe,” or “must have.” Two of these particles combine the proclitic ná with a past-tense particle, while a third combines ná with the adverb tsamʉ; these inferential forms are set on a slightly more recent time scale than the past-tense markers. The adverbs can occur either before or after the main verb.

text: Ik can also issue a confirmation of a state or event by means of a set of confirmational adverbs that are derived from the tensed relative pronouns described back in sec:5.7 . When used, these adverbs are placed before the verb, and the verb surfaces in its non-final form, almost like a question rendered in English ‘Why yes, did X not happen?’ – meaning that, of course, it did happen. These suffixes are first presented in tab:adv:conf and then demonstrated in ex:adv:11 - ex:adv:12 :
summary: The passage explains that Ik can confirm a state or event using a set of confirmational adverbs derived from the tensed relative pronouns described earlier. These adverbs occur before the verb, which appears in its non-final form, creating a meaning similar to an emphatic English question like “Why yes, did X not happen?” that actually asserts the event did happen.

text: If a state or event has not taken place but could or would take place, Ik can express that contingency with its conditional-hypothetical adverbs. There are three of these adverbs, but they are used to cover four periods of time. The first adverb covers non-past and recent past, the second removed past, and third remote past. These conditional-hypothetical adverbs are presented in tab:adv:cond : The conditional-hypothetical adverbs come after the main verb: (123)
summary: Ik uses conditional-hypothetical adverbs to express situations or events that have not occurred but could or would occur. There are three such adverbs, which together cover four time periods: the first for non-past and recent past, the second for removed past, and the third for remote past. These adverbs follow the main verb.

text: The Ik noun phrase consists first and foremost of a noun ‘head’, either a lexical noun or a nominalized lexical verb. As a head-initial language, Ik places its noun phrase head first in the phrase. Any subordinate, supporting elements follow the head. These optional elements may include anaphoric demonstratives, possessive markers, relative pronouns/temporal demonstratives, number markers, and spatial demonstratives. The Ik noun phrase structure can be formalized as follows, where elements in parentheses are optional: The syntactical structure of noun phrases formalized in ex:syn:1 is fleshed out among the real Ik noun phrases presented below in examples ex:syn:2 - ex:syn:10 :
summary: In Ik, the noun phrase is headed first by either a lexical noun or a nominalized lexical verb, reflecting the language’s head-initial word order. Any additional elements follow the head and are optional, including anaphoric demonstratives, possessive markers, relative pronouns or temporal demonstratives, number markers, and spatial demonstratives.

text: Ik intransitive clauses consist minimally of a verb (v) and a subject (s) in a vs constituent order . The subject may be explicit, in which case it follows the verb, or it may be implicit, in which case it is merely marked on the verb. Basic intransitive clause structure is illustrated in example ex:syn:11 : When a tense adverb is needed, it comes directly after the verb and before any explicit subject. And any other adverbial elements like extended objects (e) or adverbs, in that order, come after the subject. This word order is shown in ex:syn:12 :
summary: Ik intransitive clauses minimally consist of a verb and a subject in verb-subject order. The subject may be overt, following the verb, or implicit and marked on the verb; tense adverbs occur immediately after the verb and before any overt subject, while other adverbial elements such as extended objects and adverbs follow the subject.

text: Ik transitive clauses consist minimally of a transitive verb (v), an agent (a), and an object (o) in a vao constituent order . The subject may be explicit, in which case it comes between the verb and object, or it may merely be marked on the verb with a suffix. The object may also be dropped, in which case it is inferred from the context. Example ex:syn:13 illustrates basic transitive clause structure : When a tense adverb is needed, it comes directly after the verb and before any explicit subject. And any other adverbial elements like extended objects (e) or adverbs, in that order, come after the subject. This syntax is shown in ex:syn:14 :
summary: Ik transitive clauses minimally contain a transitive verb, an agent, and an object, in a vao order. The subject may be overt between the verb and object or expressed only by a verbal suffix, and the object may be omitted if recoverable from context. When present, a tense adverb follows the verb before any explicit subject, and other adverbial elements such as extended objects or adverbs come after the subject.

text: Ik ditransitive clauses consist minimally of a ditransitive verb (v), an agent (a), an object (o), and an extended object (e) in a vaoe constituent order . If the agent is not mentioned explicitly, then it will still be marked with a suffix on the verb. The object and extended object may be left implicit but will be understood from context. The basic ditransitive clause structure is illustrated in ex:syn:15 :
summary: Ik ditransitive clauses minimally contain a ditransitive verb, an agent, an object, and an extended object, in the order VAOE. If the agent is not stated overtly, it is still indicated by a suffix on the verb. The object and extended object may also be omitted when they can be inferred from context.

text: By adding an extra element in the form of a causing agent, Ik causative verbs change the structure of a clause. If the original clause was a vs intransitive one, then the causative changes it to a transitive vao. If the original clause was a transitive vao, then the causative changes it to a ditransitive vaoe. The following two examples, ex:syn:16 - ex:syn:19 , show causative verbs making these structural changes: Intransitive vs → Causative vao Transitive vao → Causative vaoe
summary: In Ik, causative verbs add a causing agent and thereby change the clause structure. An intransitive clause becomes transitive, while a transitive clause becomes ditransitive.

text: Ik has both true auxiliary verbs and pseudo-auxiliary verbs. Both types modify sentence syntax. The true auxiliaries, shown in tab:syn:aux1 , function as the syntactic main verb in a clause, while the semantic main verb follows the subject (s/a) in a morphologically defective form that consists of the bare verb stem plus a suffix -a (which may be the realis marker from sec:8.9.2 ). This means the constituent order of clauses with true auxiliary verbs is auxSV for intransitives, auxAVO for transitives, and auxAVOE with extended objects. Again, in all these constructions, the aux acts as the main verb from a syntactic perspective, while the defective verb carries the main meaning of the verbal schema. Another way to analyze this construction would be to say that the auxiliary verb and the defective verb together fill the single verb slot of the clausal syntax. The true auxiliaries have both lexical and aspectual meanings, which are nevertheless practically identical in their semantics. However, in their lexical function, the verbs in tab:syn:aux1 do not require a second, morphologically defective verb to augment them; in their strictly lexical usage, they stand alone: Example ex:syn:20 illustrates the use of the recentive aspectual auxiliary verb erúts- in an intransitive clause with the structure auxSVE: Example ex:syn:21 , on the other hand, shows the use of the anticipative verb ŋ ' ɔ r- in a transitive clause with the structure auxAVOE: Lastly, sentence ex:syn:22 exemplifies the durative aspectual verb sár- in a simple transitive clause working with the defective verb tsʼágwa-: In contrast to the above examples, the pseudo-auxiliary verbs only mimic true auxiliaries in that they are fully lexical verbs yet ones with potentially aspectual meanings, including the completive, inchoative , and occupative. However, because they are not syntactically auxiliary, they take complements as any lexical verb would (direct objects for the transitive ones and extended objects for the intransitive one). The pseudo-auxiliaries are presented in tab:syn:aux2 with their lexical and aspectual meanings and the cases required in their complements: Each of the aspectual meanings listed in tab:syn:aux2 are given one example in the following sentences. The brackets in example ex:syn:23 signify that the bracketed noun phrase as a whole is the object of the verb: Completive Inchoative Occupative
summary:
Ik distinguishes true auxiliary verbs from pseudo-auxiliaries, and both affect clause syntax. True auxiliaries function as the syntactic main verb while a following morphologically defective verb in bare-stem plus -a form carries the main verbal meaning, yielding orders such as auxSV, auxAVO, and auxAVOE; these auxiliary verbs can also occur as ordinary lexical verbs without the defective verb.  

Pseudo-auxiliaries, by contrast, are fully lexical verbs with possible aspectual meanings such as completive, inchoative, and occupative, but they are not syntactic auxiliaries and therefore take their complements like other lexical verbs.

text: Ik copular clauses have relational rather than referential meanings. They link a copular subject (cs) to a copular complement (cc) which represents an entity or attribute, depending on the specific copular verb involved. The constituent order of copular clauses is therefore v-cs-cc. Ik has three distinct copular or ‘be’ verbs that can express five copular relationships between them. These copular verbs are presented in tab:syn:cop below, along with the case markings their subjects and complements are obligated to have: The three copular verbs in tab:syn:cop and their five potential meaning are each exemplified briefly in the example sentences ex:syn:26 - ex:syn:30 : Existence Location Attribution Identity Possession
summary: Copular clauses in Ik have relational rather than referential meanings, linking a copular subject to a copular complement that denotes either an entity or an attribute, with the basic order v-cs-cc. Ik has three distinct copular “be” verbs, which together express five copular relations: existence, location, attribution, identity, and possession, each with specific obligatory case markings on the subject and complement.

text: Ik can put special emphasis on any core nominal element by moving it to the front of the clause, before the verb, subject, and other constituents. Doing so obviously disrupts the usual syntactic structure of main clauses. Two kinds of fronting are observed in the language: 1) a cleft construction and 2) left-dislocation. In a cleft construction , the emphasized noun is moved to the front and given the copulative case . This puts it in an identifying relationship with the original clause out of which it just came. As a result, the newly arranged clause can be viewed as a kind of copular clause where the fronted element is the copular subject and the original clause the copular complement . This can in turn be formulized as: [NP:cop] cs [clause] cc . To make this more concrete, the next examples show the cleft construction with a simple transitive clause in ex:syn:31 whose object ( m ` ɛ s ) gets fronted and marked with the copulative case in ex:syn:32 : Cleft construction Whereas the cleft construction involves removing a clausal element from a clause and building a new clause, left-dislocation simply relocates the element to the front of the clause, but still within the same clause. In this fronted position it is given the nominative case . This type of fronting can be formulized as: [NP:nom ‖ clause] clause , where the double vertical line symbolize a short pause. This type of left-dislocation is illustrated between example sentences ex:syn:33 - ex:syn:34 : Left-dislocation
summary: The passage explains that Ik can mark special emphasis by fronting a core nominal element before the verb, subject, and other constituents, although this disrupts the normal clause structure. It distinguishes two kinds of fronting: cleft construction, in which the fronted noun is removed from the original clause and marked with copulative case as part of a copular-like structure, and left-dislocation, in which the noun is simply moved to the front within the same clause and marked with nominative case.

text: The constituent order of Ik subordinate clauses differs from that of main clauses. Ik subordinate clauses exhibit an sv order with intransitive verbs, an av order with transitives, and an ave order with ditransitives – in short ‘sv’ instead of the usual ‘vs’. Case marking in subordinate clauses is also different: The fronted subject/agent and every direct object take the accusative case . The next two subsections deal with two key kinds of Ik subordinate clause , the relative clause ( sec:10.3.2 ) and the adverbial clause ( sec:10.3.3 ).
summary: Ik subordinate clauses have a different constituent order from main clauses: intransitives show sv order, transitives av, and ditransitives ave, instead of the usual vs pattern. Their case marking also differs, since the fronted subject/agent and every direct object take accusative case. The passage then introduces two major types of subordinate clause: relative clauses and adverbial clauses.

text: relative clauses are subordinate clauses that modify a noun within a main clause . Ik relative clauses are restrictive, meaning they can only narrow the reference of their head noun rather than merely adding extra details about it. Relative clauses are introduced by the tensed relative pronouns discussed back in ( sec:5.7 ), which, within the relative clause , stand in for a noun in the main clause called the common argument (ca). As such, the common argument is a full verbal argument in the main clause , while in the relative clause , the relative pronoun fills its syntactic slot. As a subordinate clause , an Ik relative clause exhibits a different constituent order than typical main clauses. Specifically, an intransitive relative clause has the order sv (instead of vs), and a transitive relative clause has the order oav (instead of vao). In the former ( intransitive ), the subject slot (s) is filled by the relative pronoun , and in the latter (transitive), it is the object (o) that is represented by the relative pronoun . Furthermore, apart for the relative pronouns themselves, all subjects and direct objects in relative clauses are marked with the accusative case – another sign of grammatical subordination in Ik. These attributes of Ik relative clauses are illustrated in examples ex:syn:35 - ex:syn:36 . In ex:syn:35 , the common argument in the main clause is emuta ‘story’, which is modified by the relative clause nɛ ' ɛ f ‘that is funny’. Note how the subject slot of the relative clause is filled by the relative pronoun nɛ (na with its vowel assimilated). Then, in ex:syn:36 , the common argument of the main clause is ima ‘child’, modified by the relative clause náa ɲcia tákí ‘that I mentioned’. Since the verb of the relative clause is transitive (tákés ‘to mean, mention’), it requires an object, which in this case is fulfilled by the relative pronoun náa representing the noun ima: Intransitive (sv) Transitive (oav)
summary: Ik relative clauses are restrictive subordinate clauses that modify a noun in the main clause, with a tensed relative pronoun filling the position of the noun it represents in the relative clause. Because they are subordinate, they show different word order from main clauses: intransitive relative clauses have sv order and transitive relative clauses have oav order, with subjects and direct objects generally marked by the accusative case.

text: The category of adverbial clauses is rather broad as it includes any subordinate clause that modifies a main clause adverbially.
